title: Sunscreen Reforms Proposed After 16 of 20 Products Fail SPF Tests - Retail News Asia

 By Wei Zhang Australia 2 min read Publication date: Oct 28, 2026 7:19 AM Share | Save In this article ( 9 ) In this article
 Mandatory Testing Shifts Before Shelf Placement

 Questions & Answers 
 What triggered the regulatory overhaul by the Therapeutic Goods Administration? 
 What new testing rules will manufacturers have to follow before selling sunscreens? 
 Why has the regulator decided against creating a public database of test results? 
 How are the proposed changes expected to affect retailers and smaller beauty labels? 
 Australia’s Therapeutic Goods Administration is overhauling sunscreen testing rules, requiring brands to conduct repeated SPF verification and lodge data before products reach retail shelves.
 The regulatory shift follows testing conducted last year that discovered 16 out of 20 popular sunscreen formulations failed to deliver their claimed sun protection factor.
 Consumer advocacy group Choice, industry body Accord Australasia and the Australian Sunscreen Association have backed elements of the framework while demanding that the TGA scrutinise the compliance costs and supply availability before codifying the rules. Under the proposed regime, personal care manufacturers must test finished shelf formulations rather than base batches, repeating trials across the stated shelf life of the product.
 Mandatory Testing Shifts Before Shelf Placement
 Brands currently sell sunscreens in Australia without lodging baseline laboratory data with the regulator prior to retail distribution unless specifically ordered to produce records. The updated rules eliminate that gap by forcing suppliers to lodge certified testing dossiers with the TGA ahead of retail launch.
 Laboratory evaluation protocols will also change to accommodate in vitro testing methods conducted on plates rather than relying solely on human volunteer skin trials. The TGA confirmed human testing protocols will remain compulsory for specific categories, including water-resistant claims, to prevent degradation under real-world conditions.
 The regulator decided against establishing an open public registry of brand testing results. Officials cited commercial confidentiality, trade secret protections and the risk that technical testing metrics would confuse shoppers.
 “ Suppliers face sharp operational cost increases as testing requirements expand from one-off formula verifications to continuous stability batches. ” 
 Supply Chain Friction for Beauty and Personal Care Brands
 RetailNews Asia sees this regulatory clampdown reshaping procurement margins for pharmacy chains, beauty retailers, and contract manufacturers across the Asia-Pacific region. Australia represents the strictest suncare compliance market in the southern hemisphere, and Australian compliance frequently serves as the quality benchmark for brands exporting into Southeast Asian retail networks.
 Suppliers face sharp operational cost increases as testing requirements expand from one-off formula verifications to continuous stability batches. Independent indie brands and cross-border beauty labels using third-party contract packagers will bear the brunt of these overheads, creating shelf consolidation in major retailers such as Coles, Woolworths, and chemist chains.
 Fallout from Sunscreen Recalls
 The regulatory overhaul stems from an industry crisis when independent testing showed severe disparities between front-label claims and actual barrier performance. One mineral sunscreen labelled SPF 50+ registered a protection score of just SPF 4 during laboratory trials, triggering a recall of the product alongside 19 sister formulations built on the identical base matrix.
 While products like Mecca Cosmetica’s To Save Body SPF 50+ recorded matching protection levels of SPF 51 in the same trial, the wider category suffered severe reputational erosion. The TGA’s chief medical adviser, Professor Robyn Langham, explained that investigations revealed multiple systemic factors behind failing batches rather than isolated formulation errors.
 Australians expect the SPF on the label to be backed by robust evidence. These proposed reforms put that expectation at the centre of sunscreen regulation.
 Next Regulatory Steps and Compliance Milestones
 The TGA will review submissions from retail and chemical industry groups regarding cost burdens before finalising the regulatory timetable. Consumer advocates continue to demand that the regulator institute an independent government-run batch testing programme rather than relying exclusively on company filings.
 Beauty retailers and FMCG distributors operating across Australia and regional export markets are now auditing supplier dossiers ahead of the binding implementation dates.

 Q. What triggered the regulatory overhaul by the Therapeutic Goods Administration?
 A. Testing revealed that 16 out of 20 popular sunscreen formulations failed their stated sun protection factor, including an SPF 50+ mineral lotion that scored just SPF 4. These failures prompted widespread product recalls and damaged consumer confidence across the wider category.
 Q. What new testing rules will manufacturers have to follow before selling sunscreens?
 A. Brands will need to test finished shelf formulations rather than base batches and repeat these trials across product shelf life. They must also submit certified testing dossiers to the regulator before retail distribution, using in vitro methods alongside mandatory human trials for water-resistant claims.
 Q. Why has the regulator decided against creating a public database of test results?
 A. The Therapeutic Goods Administration decided against a public register to protect trade secrets and commercial confidentiality. Officials also determined that releasing technical testing metrics could confuse consumers trying to choose appropriate sun protection products.
 Q. How are the proposed changes expected to affect retailers and smaller beauty labels?
 A. Operational costs will rise as testing shifts from one-off verifications to continuous stability batches. These overheads will heavily affect independent brands and contract packagers, potentially causing shelf consolidation across major supermarkets like Coles and Woolworths as well as chemist chains.
